title: Can’t Name It, Can’t Log Off: Alexithymia and Problematic Internet-Related Behaviors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Fangqing Liu, Xiaoshan Yin
abstract: Alexithymia has been proposed as a ransdiagnostic vulnerability for behavioral addictions, but its role in problematic Internet-related behaviors (PIB) has not been quantified across phenotypes and populations. We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses. Major databases were searched in October 2025 for studies reporting quantitative associations between alexithymia and PIB (problematic Internet, smartphone, social media, gaming use, or cyberbullying). Risk of bias was appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Random-effects models pooled correlations and standardized regression coefficients; three-level and robust-variance models accounted for multiple effects per study and examined moderators and adjustment for internalizing symptoms. Eighty-three studies met inclusion criteria; 78 independent samples ( N = 42,478; 369 effect sizes total, comprising 302 zero-order correlations and 67 standardized regression coefficients) contributed to the meta-analysis. The pooled correlation between alexithymia and PIB was r = 0.36 (95% confidence interval 0.34–0.38; I 2 = 77.6%). Associations were stronger for addictive-use PIB ( r = 0.37) than for cyberbullying ( r = 0.29), broadly comparable across world regions, and tended to be larger in adults than adolescents. In multivariable models, coefficients attenuated from about β = 0.37 to β = 0.18 after controlling for depression, anxiety, and other internalizing symptoms, but remained statistically significant. Sensitivity and publication-bias analyses indicated that the association was robust. Alexithymia shows a moderate association with PIB across age groups, partly via shared variance with internalizing psychopathology but also through unique pathways. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies should test whether targeting emotional awareness can help prevent or reduce PIB.

title: Public reactions on TikTok: Emotional dynamics in comments to the president of Romania's posts
authors: Tănase Tasențe, Cristina-Dana Popescu
abstract: This article examines how TikTok structures the emotional dynamics of presidential communication during the initial months of a mandate, focusing on the official account of the President of Romania. Drawing on 44 TikTok posts and 29,756 unique public comments recorded between 26 May and 27 October 2025, the study combines multilingual transformer-based sentiment analysis, change-point analysis and co-commenting network analysis. After deduplication and temporal filtering, 21,654 comments were classified. The results show a positive plurality rather than a uniformly positive baseline, alongside issue-specific negativity around economic governance, justice and public safety, security, Moldova and democratic legitimacy. Validation sensitivity checks caution against strong comment-level claims, whilst a bipartite null model shows that much co-commenting density is expected from shared participation in viral threads. TikTok is therefore interpreted as a high-co-presence environment in which episodic affective pressure emerges around salient political themes.

title: From prompt to profession: how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability through skill development
authors: Bahar Javadi Khasraghi, Qiuli Su, Hanieh Javadi Khasraghi
abstract: Purpose The proliferation of generative AI tools like ChatGPT is transforming higher education, yet evidence of their impact on students' career readiness remains limited. Existing studies often rely on localized samples and emphasize usage frequency over underlying mechanisms. This study investigates how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability, focusing on perceived proficiency (e.g. writing, communication) and analytical skills (e.g. critical thinking, problem-solving) as mediators. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Self-Perception Theory and Human Capital Theory, with the Technology Acceptance Model providing a conceptual starting point for understanding technology engagement, we use structural equation modeling (SEM) to analyze survey data from 21,716 students across 100 countries, examining associations among ChatGPT use, perceived proficiency and analytical skill development, and perceived employability, with mediation through the two skills. Findings ChatGPT use is positively associated with both skill domains; however, only perceived proficiency is significantly associated with perceived employability. The indirect effect via proficiency is significant, whereas the indirect effect via analytical skills is not, and the direct path from ChatGPT use to employability is nonsignificant, consistent with a full-mediation model. Multi-group analyses indicate stronger effects for students from low- and lower-middle-income countries and for female students, with no substantive differences by field of study. Originality/value This study provides large-scale, theory-driven evidence linking ChatGPT use to perceived skill development and employability. These findings suggest that structured, critical engagement with AI tools may support skill development without displacing deeper learning. It offers critical insights for higher education policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era.

title: Identity and Words: Does Gender-Fair Language Impact Workers’ Gender-Work Identity Integration?
authors: Claudia Manzi, Eleonora Crapolicchio, Valeria Amata Giannella, Maria Giuseppina Pacilli, Gabriele Di Cicco, Verónica Benet-Martínez
abstract: Understanding how individuals integrate their work and non-work identities has become a central concern in research analyzing individual differences in the work context. In particular, gender-work identity integration (GWII) has been proven to significantly impact employee well-being and work adjustment. We present two studies designed to improve GWII by gender-fair language use at work. In Study 1 ( N = 1024), employees of a telecommunication company, after completing a pre-test, received instructions to use either double gender-marking language (DGML, N = 355) or gender-neutral language (GNL, N = 310) in written communication. A third control group ( N = 359) did not receive any instructions. Results show that use of DGML improved employees’ GWII over time, which, in turn, also increased their work engagement and well-being. Study 2 ( N = 219) replicated findings from Study 1 showing that change in DGML use improves GWII, but only under low levels of observed sexist behaviors in the organization. Together, these findings provide evidence of the impact of organizational language policies on employees’ identity processes and well-being.
journal_full: Journal of Language and Social Psychology

title: ChangeMyView: Unpacking the Complex Emotional, Cognitive, and Communicator-Related Processes Underlying Persuasion
authors: Isabella M. Swafford, Alfonso Carballo, Ryan L. Boyd, Vanessa Kountakis, Lucy McGregor, Vivian P. Ta-Johnson
abstract: Persuasion is shaped by complex emotional triggers, cognitive reasoning, and communicator-related characteristics. However, theories of persuasion have often examined different features of persuasive communication in controlled research settings, resulting in questions about how these characteristics exist within naturally occurring persuasive messages. This study addresses this gap by examining theoretically relevant linguistic characteristics associated with successful persuasion using r/ChangeMyView , an online debate forum where users attempt to change others’ views on any topic, and posts resulting in successful persuasion are marked. In Study 1, Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count was used to analyze n = 9020 r/ChangeMyView posts from 2013 to 2018. Principal component analyses identified three broad linguistic dimensions reflecting cognitive reasoning, emotional expression, and authentic communication style. These components were then entered into a multilevel logistic regression analysis, revealing that greater scores on the cognitive reasoning dimension were associated with lower persuasive likelihood, whereas emotional expression and authentic communication were not significantly associated with persuasion. Study 2 analyzed 51,394 posts from 2019 to 2023 and identified a similar three-component structure, demonstrating consistency in how the selected linguistic characteristics grouped across samples. Cognitive reasoning again predicted lower persuasive likelihood, while greater emotional expression predicted lower persuasive likelihood and authentic communication predicted greater persuasive likelihood. The results suggest that naturally occurring persuasive language organizes into reproducible but nuanced dimensions, and that multiple forms of linguistic information contribute to persuasive messaging. Overall, the findings provide naturalistic evidence relevant to theoretical accounts that conceptualize persuasion as involving multiple, potentially overlapping forms of information processing.
journal_full: Journal of Language and Social Psychology

title: What Makes Child Harm Newsworthy? Event Characteristics, Victim Characteristics, and Media Attention
authors: Nikolay Ternov, Kuralay Mukhambetova, Zeinep Abetova
abstract: Media coverage shapes public understanding of social problems, yet harmful events receive uneven attention even when they involve children. This study examines factors shaping media visibility of child harm in Kazakhstan. Using a corpus of more than 230,000 Telegram news posts (2020–2025), we identify 1,571 incidents involving harm to children and estimate negative binomial regression models to test explanations derived from news values and ideal victim theory. Results show that event characteristics predict media attention more strongly than victim characteristics. Fatal interpersonal violence receives more coverage, while systemic failures receive less. Victim age and gender are not significant predictors.

title: Stories that Make Hawks? Digital News-Based User-Generated Content and Foreign Policy Orientations Among China’s Generation Z
authors: Yang Li, Ying Hooi Khoo, Siti Ezaleila Binti Mustafa
abstract: This study examines the relationships between exposure to news-based user-generated content on Bilibili and Chinese Generation Z’s support for hawkish foreign policies. Guided by the Narrative Policy Framework, a survey ( N = 688) shows that self-reported exposure to villain, hero, and mixed narrative strategies is positively associated with hawkish orientations, both directly and indirectly through national pride and national humiliation. These findings suggest that, within the highly performative and affectively embedded dynamics of social media, nonofficial actors may rely on dramatized storytelling and serve as a nonnegligible component of the broader rise of hawkishness within Chinese youth communities.

title: Texting for Connection in an “Always-On” Society: Roles of Content, Availability Pressure, and Emotional Fatigue
authors: David de Segovia Vicente, Mariek M. P. Vanden Abeele, Kyle Van Gaeveren, Stephen Murphy, Jeffrey A. Hall
abstract: Texting is the most ubiquitous form of computer-mediated communication, but its ability to satisfy relational needs in an always-on society remains under scrutiny. This study examines how message content and psychological context—specifically emotional fatigue and availability pressure—determine the relational value of texting. Analyzing 5,821 ecological momentary assessments from 112 adults, the results reveal that while texting and offline interactions positively predict connectedness, offline interactions demonstrate a meaningfully stronger effect. Within the context of texting, meaningful and affectionate interactions are associated with high levels of connectedness compared with those of small talk or practical exchanges, supporting the hierarchy of communication episodes proposed by communicate bond belong theory. Notably, neither emotional fatigue nor availability pressure significantly influences the association between texting and connectedness. These findings highlight that the relational benefits of texting are resilient to emotional fatigue and availability pressure and primarily depend on the nature of the content instead of users' psychological context.

title: Stress and self-efficacy under artificial intelligence disruption: A mixed-methods study on the usage of artificial intelligence among Finnish workers
authors: Atte Oksanen, Teo Keipi, Moona Heiskari, Iina Savolainen
abstract: Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.

title: Norwegian party leaders’ communication on social media platforms during Covid-19 lockdowns: A longitudinal comparison of Facebook and Instagram content
authors: Roy Aulie Jacobsen
abstract: Social media platforms became key channels for political leaders’ crisis communication during the Covid-19 pandemic. In this article, I examine how Norwegian party leaders used Facebook and Instagram across three national lockdowns in Norway. A dataset of 2,397 posts from national party leaders was coded using a four-part framework for analysing government communication on social media platforms, capturing information provision, input-seeking, politics, and symbolic presentation. Post-level linear probability models estimate how the probability of each communication type varied by platform and lockdown period, controlling for government or opposition status and Covid-19 relatedness. Facebook accounts for a larger share of posts and carries a broader crisis-communication repertoire, particularly for political and input-seeking communication. The use of Instagram for crisis communication became more selective over time, with several communication types declining during the third lockdown. Contrary to participatory expectations, input-seeking decreased as the crisis persisted. Opposition leaders relied more on information provision across platforms, consistent with visibility and accountability work during prolonged crisis governance.

title: Why research on science communication needs more meta-analyses
authors: Niels G. Mede, Mike S. Schäfer, Elisa Tedaldi
abstract: Research on science communication has expanded and diversified. Correspondingly, an increasing number of literature reviews, handbooks, and bibliometric studies have taken stock of the field’s accumulated knowledge. However, it is still difficult to identify robust, consolidated answers to key questions on science communication—answers that may help scholars, practitioners, and decision-makers. Meta-analyses—the statistical aggregation of empirical results across multiple studies to determine average effect sizes—can provide some of those answers, complementing existing knowledge syntheses and addressing their shortcomings. Yet, meta-analyses in research on science communication are rare, whereas other disciplines are much closer to establishing a culture of meta-analyses and demonstrate the usefulness of meta-analyses for specific aspects of science communication research within and beyond our discipline. We therefore propose a meta-analytical research agenda of science communication scholarship and argue that it will increase the impact of our field in the social sciences and society.

title: Webs of Ainu Mosir: Indigenous Creative Networks on YouTube
authors: Xanat Vargas Meza, Takumi Yokoyama, Chieko Nishimura, Ryohei Nishida, Yoichi Ochiai
abstract: The Ainu are Indigenous people living primarily in Japan. As they have recently adopted social media, and network-based analyses of First Nations cultural manifestations are uncommon, this study drew on Indigenous and social network frameworks to examine creative networks in the virtual Mosir (the world as viewed by the Ainu). Our objective was to clarify the types of collaborators, their cooperation patterns and relationships relevant to producing Ainu-related YouTube videos. Three YouTube lists of 428 videos were utilised in this study. Publicly available data were downloaded using a YouTube Application Programming Interface (API). The videos were watched and classified, including anonymised data on collaborators. The relationships of the collaborators were quantified and mapped, network measurements were calculated and collaborator clusters were examined. The most frequent types of collaborators were individuals and communities. We also observed that individuals moderately affected network clustering ( p = .002). Furthermore, individuals were somewhat correlated with the average number of ties ( p = .004) and the bridging of clusters through betweenness ( p = .006), with Japanese male celebrities and Ainu people, particularly Ainu women, showing high centrality. As Indigenous rights advance internationally, the virtual Mosir shows how crucial it is for First Nations to participate in multimedia production processes, particularly if such productions are available on social media. Indigenous network frameworks were highly compatible with network analysis, allowing for a more comprehensive overview of Indigenous production processes. This can enhance the multiple knowledges of First Nations, while fostering accountability and reciprocity of their allies.

title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
authors: Linda Li, Helen Margetts
abstract: Social bots are an increasingly prominent presence in online protest discourse. We adapt the discursive opportunity structure (DOS) framework for digital protest, refining its dimensions of visibility, resonance and legitimacy to account for platform-mediated discourse and automated activity. Applying the refined framework through computer-assisted content analysis of bot activity in two major protests – Black Lives Matter (BLM) and Extinction Rebellion (XR) – we move beyond treating bots as a monolithic or uniformly disruptive force, identifying competing pro- and counter-protest strategies distributed differently across the three dimensions. In BLM, pro-protest bot content concentrates on cultural resonance, whereas counter-bot content targets legitimacy; in XR, pro-protest bots are used to build legitimacy and participatory visibility, whereas counter-bots more often work to downplay the movement’s salience. The framework’s granularity discriminates between movement types in ways coarser accounts of ‘political bots’ cannot, showing that understanding contemporary movements requires attending to how automated activity is deployed within their discourse.

title: How Personal Curation Shapes Political Engagement on Social Media? Examining The Politics of Personal Curation Model
authors: Biying Wu-Ouyang
abstract: Although individuals today have a wide range of media choices to engage in politics, recent investigations have revealed that many are increasingly avoiding news and disengaging from politics, especially in social media. From a user-centered perspective, few effective strategies on social media have been systematically examined to enhance political engagement. Established through the curated flows framework, this study proposes the Politics of Personal Curation (PPC) model, which offers a fresh perspective by examining how everyday mundane personal curation in social media (platform expansiveness, content heterogeneity, news attentiveness, and source belongingness curation) have significantly influences on political engagement. A preregistered study from a nationally representative panel in the United States ( N = 1,270) generally indicates that expansiveness, heterogeneity, and news attentiveness curation yield higher political engagement, whereas belongingness curation is linked to lower engagement. This study further supports that these media effects on political engagement are channeled through enhanced cognitive elaboration and moderated by cross-cutting discussion.

title: Television Time and Electoral Success: Evidence From the Constitutional Convention Election in Chile in 2021
authors: Roberto Munita-Morgan, Patricio Navia
abstract: Some democracies give all political parties free television time to level the electoral campaign playing field. Relying on a case that uses open-list proportional representation rules and where voters select individual candidates, but where free television time is assigned to party lists, we explore the association between appearing in free television ads (franja) and electoral success in Chile’s 2021 Constitutional Convention election. In this unprecedented contest, airtime was allocated to parties and lists of independents. We use an original coding of 3,157 mentions across 28 days of television ads for candidates in the four largest electoral lists (692 candidates). Candidates mentioned in ads received higher vote shares (2.9 vs. 2.2 percent) and were more likely to win seats (18.6 vs. 7.7 percent). Multivariate models show that campaign spending is more strongly associated with electoral success, but mentions in the franja have a modest but statistically significant positive coefficient. Although we cannot disentangle the potential endogeneity of being more electable and appearing in the franja, the findings highlight the importance of television time for electoral success and point to how party-controlled media exposure influences intra-list competition.

title: Digital turnout mobilization: Enhancing voter turnout with digital messaging
authors: Kasper M. Hansen, Esther Ejrnæs Bastholm
abstract: Voter turnout is declining across Europe, raising concerns about democratic legitimacy and prompting a search for effective mobilization strategies. The new digital era has transformed the landscape for political communication, making it possible to mobilize voters through direct digital messages. These messages have proven to be a low-cost and easily scalable tool, capable of reaching millions of voters efficiently and with broad coverage. We synthesize existing evidence through a comprehensive meta-analysis of voter mobilization experiments from the past decade that apply digital messages as a Get-Out-The-Vote (GOTV) tool. The analysis assesses the overall effectiveness of digital messaging in increasing turnout, with particular attention to its potential for engaging marginalized groups and promoting participatory equality. Second, we present results from a new population-wide GOTV experiment conducted during the 2024 European Parliament election in Denmark – the first to apply digital messages to the entire electorate. The intervention increased turnout by 0.5 percentage points. By using year-of-birth bins to estimate effects across all age cohorts and disaggregating the immigrant category into Western and non-Western subpopulations, we can examine previously unexplored in-depth heterogeneous effects. We find that digital messages consistently have positive effects on turnout, including among marginalized voters.

title: Strategic alienation: The dynamics of group appeals in negative campaigning
authors: Lena Maria Huber, Martin Haselmayer
abstract: This paper examines how political parties use social group appeals in negative campaigning. We argue that parties strategically target opponents with group-based attacks to portray them as failing key social groups. Using a novel dataset of Facebook and Twitter posts by parties in the UK (2016–2024), linked to voter perceptions of group representation from the British Election Study, we test whether such attacks are more likely when the sender party enjoys strong group-based credibility, or the target party is seen as a weak representative of the respective group, or both. We find no evidence for the former but strong support for the latter: parties disproportionately target rivals with poor reputations for representing specific groups, and especially so when the sender holds a reputational advantage. These findings advance our understanding of identity-driven party competition, showing that group-based attacks exploit opponents’ representational vulnerabilities rather than reinforce attackers’ own strength.

title: Using Television Drama to Promote Electoral Corruption Reporting: An Evaluation in Northern Nigeria
authors: Dan Brown, Ariel Lee Bothen, Michelle Krieger, Fatima Turaki, Mansur Kurugu, Maji Peterx, Catherine Angai, Ummi Yakubu, Vanessa Alli
abstract: We evaluated an edutainment intervention to encourage electoral corruption reporting in northern Nigeria via a live broadcast of a popular Hausa-language TV show, which aired October–December 2022, shortly before the February 2023 presidential elections. We incorporated behaviorally informed anticorruption messages into the scripts of the TV drama to encourage its tens of millions of viewers to report instances of electoral corruption. We used a randomized encouragement trial design, sampling over 6,000 participants across northern Nigeria through pre-recorded phone surveys. Watching the show caused a statistically significant increase in the perceived helpfulness and frequency of reporting, but we could not detect changes in knowledge of how to report or reporting behaviors.

title: The Synthetic Imputation Approach: Using LLMs to Generate Synthetic Texts for Underrepresented Categories in Supervised Classification Tasks
authors: Joan C. Timoneda
abstract: Annotated text data are central to many empirical applications in political science, yet many annotation tasks involve categories that are sparsely populated. These low- N categories pose problems for both encoder-only and decoder-only (generative) Transformer large language models (LLMs), leading to low performance, biased evaluation and measurement error in downstream analyses. This article introduces the synthetic imputation approach, a targeted method for expanding sparse categories while remaining consistent with the category-defining content of the human-coded examples. The approach uses a generative LLM to produce additional texts for underrepresented categories by conditioning on small, rotating subsets of human-coded examples. Rather than paraphrasing or replacing the original data, synthetic imputation adds informative variation only where data are thin. I evaluate the approach using both encoder-only and decoder-only LLM classifiers across multiple political science applications. The results show that synthetic imputation substantially improves performance and evaluation stability in sparse settings, recovering full-sample performance once a modest number of true observations is available, with limited and predictable overfitting at very low levels of N .

title: From misogyny to mobilization: Hostile sexism and conflictual online discussions indirectly predict men's rights activism via heightened identification as a men's rights supporter
authors: Morgana Lizzio‐Wilson, Emma F. Thomas, Cassandra M. Quarisa, Anna C. Barron, Danny Osborne
abstract: Although sexism may serve as a gateway into the men's rights movement, few studies have examined group processes in online environments that fuel this reactionary movement. We address this gap by examining whether interacting with like‐minded others fosters an emergent social identity as a “men's rights supporter” among sexist men; and whether identification predicts willingness to engage in reactionary actions undermining gender equality. Across two studies ( N s = 443, 755), men completed a hostile sexism measure and read about the perceived impacts of feminism on men. Participants then either discussed whether feminism negatively impacts men in an online chatroom (group deliberation) or reflected individually (individual deliberation). Hostile sexism predicted identification as a men's rights supporter, and this link was stronger in the group deliberation condition. In turn, identification predicted greater reactionary action intentions. Unexpectedly, these effects emerged only among men who indicated that their group was unsure about the impact of feminism after the discussion. A post‐hoc content analysis of the pooled chat logs revealed that these men engaged in discussions marked by conflict and disagreement, suggesting that identification with the movement emerged through dissent rather than consensus. These findings highlight complex social dynamics underpinning engagement with the men's rights movement.

title: Big Tech, big risk? How education and ideology shape public attitudes toward Big Tech companies
authors: Tobias Tober, Marius R. Busemeyer, Sebastian Koos
abstract: This paper examines public attitudes toward Big Tech and their relationship to policy preferences in six OECD countries. Drawing on original survey data collected in 2022 from 19,800 respondents in Germany, Japan, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and the United States, we analyze how education and political ideology shape evaluations of large technology firms such as Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft. Using six survey items on the perceived economic, social, and democratic effects of Big Tech, we identify two weakly correlated attitudinal dimensions: positive and negative evaluations. A cluster analysis reveals five groups of respondents—supporters, skeptics, ambivalent, dismissive, and neutral—highlighting that public opinion on Big Tech is not organized along a single continuum. Bayesian multinomial regression models show that higher education is associated less with outright support than with greater ambivalence, while ideology structures attitudes in distinct ways: skepticism is more pronounced on the left, whereas ambivalence rises especially among highly educated respondents on the right. These attitudinal clusters are closely linked to preferences for regulation and government support. The findings suggest that public opinion toward Big Tech is complex, politically structured, and consequential for policy debates.

title: Who Is Afraid of ChatGPT? A Natural Experiment on the Effect of ChatGPT Release on Labour-Market Concerns
authors: Francesco Nicoli, Gregorio Buzzelli, Brian Burgoon, Stefano Sacchi
abstract: The public release of ChatGPT on November 30th, 2022 revived the public debate on technological change and, particularly, on its impact on the labour market. Despite the sudden growth in AI salience after the launch of the new chatbot, to our knowledge, no empirical investigation has assessed the impact of this technological breakthrough on citizens’ first concerns. By means of a unique survey fielded between November and December 2022 in five European countries, we use an Unexpected Event During Survey (UEDS) design to causally test the effect of ChatGPT’s launch on individual perception of unemployment risk. We rely on statistical matching techniques, combined with regression analyses to explore heterogeneity in responses between socioeconomic groups. We show that the release of the new chatbot mildly but significantly increased unemployment concerns in advanced industrial democracies, particularly among individuals with low and middling levels of income and education, as well as poorly exposed to AI. By capturing reactions before informational framings consolidate and widespread adoption occurs, this study provides a rare window into citizens’ genuine response to technological change, indicating that its socioeconomic consequences are perceived as immediately salient.

title: Role-Playing as Immigrants for Learning to Trust: Constructing a Theory of Experiential Contact
authors: Brandon C. Bouchillon
abstract: This research examined whether a computer-based role-playing game in which participants created immigrant characters from Mexico and took them through the process of naturalizing to the United States could be used to promote trust. A posttest-only experiment with a control group was conducted in Fall 2024 ( N = 98). Results indicate that participants who played the game had significantly higher levels of trust in immigrants in general, as well as those from Mexico, Central/South America, India, China, and the Middle East specifically, compared to the control condition. Parasocial connections to characters in game-based settings strengthened the effect of role-playing on trusting immigrants from Mexico. Half of the role-playing participants also saw a thank-you video from an outgroup representative, as a form of mediated indirect contact. The video condition appeared to drive the interaction between role-playing and sensing parasocial connections to characters in predicting Mexican immigrant trust. Results demonstrate the potential for role-playing games to foster trust between groups who may struggle to interact in person, along with the additive effect of mediated indirect contact at high levels of parasocial connection.

title: Estimating the threat of AI-agent responding across online survey platforms
authors: Grace Zhang, Robert Walatka, Stephanie Y. Chen, Alexander K. Moore, Oleg Urminsky, Kianté Fernandez, Andrea Low, Jonathan E. Bogard, Craig R. Fox
abstract: Recent research and advances in LLMs have led to widespread concern that AI agents could pose as human online survey-takers. However, it remains unclear how prevalent AI agents are on survey research platforms and how to effectively detect AI agents. We validated a series of AI detection tests that effectively separated verified-human participants from both prompted commercial and purpose-built AI agents. Using these tests, we collected surveys on seven online platforms and find wide variation in rates of respondents failing AI tests, ranging from 6 to 41% across platforms (compared to a 2.4% false-positive rate for in-person human participants). We further demonstrate that undetected AI agents can impact the results of online surveys. Our findings suggest that while there is an urgent need for AI detection tests and consistent, systematic monitoring of data quality on online platforms, some platforms currently appear to provide data with a low rate of AI agents.
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
authors: Nicolò Pagan, Petter Törnberg, Christopher A. Bail, Christopher Barrie
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
